# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Associative forward blocking[^1] refers to the attenuation of learning
about a stimulus-outcome relationship when the stimulus is accompanied
by another one that has already been established to reliably predict
that outcome [@beesley2011; @paskewitz2020].

[^1]: Herein, I will refer to forward blocking simply as *blocking* to
    avoid text cluttering. However, note that other forms, such as
    backward blocking, whereby learning stages of are reversed starting
    with compound cues followed by single-cue contingencies, were also
    defined.

Behavioural studies combined with eye-tracking have demonstrated that
blocking occurs in human associative learning and that it can be
accounted for by learned *in*attention to the blocked cue
[@kruschke2005; @beesley2011; @lepelley2007; @wills2007; @luque2018].
Two candidate mechanisms have been proposed to explain this phenomenon:
rapid **attentional shifts**, whereby redirecting attention away from
the blocked cue improves learning, and **attentional competition**,
whereby cues vie for a limited attentional resource [@kruschke2005;
@paskewitz2020].

However, no definitive experiment capable of discriminating between
these two proposed mechanisms has yet been conducted. Using simulations,
@paskewitz2020 derived an experimental design that could, in principle,
adjudicate between the two accounts.

The primary aims of this project are to:

1.  *replicate* the prototypical blocking findings of @beesley2011 in a
    large sample, and
2.  *design and implement an extension* of this paradigm that allows for
    direct comparison between the attentional shift and attentional
    competition accounts of blocking, drawing on the theoretical
    analysis by @paskewitz2020.

## Forward Blocking {#sec-history}

Blocking was first described in rodents by @kamin1969 and later
demonstrated in human contingency learning by @dickinson1984 and
@shanks1985. The basic phenomenon can be explained by simple associative
learning models such as the Rescorla–Wagner model [@rescorla1972].
However, subsequent work suggested that blocking is accompanied by
shifts of attention away from blocked cues, and can thus be better
explained by attentional theories of associative learning [e.g.,
@mackintosh1975; @pearce1980].

Although alternative explanations based on propositional reasoning have
been proposed ***(cite propositional theories)***, learned attention
accounts remain influential and continue to be used in both empirical
and computational work [@paskewitz2020; @paskewitz2023; @kelly2025a;
@kelly2025b][^2]. Rather than adjudicating directly between competing
theoretical frameworks, the present study focuses on subjecting learned
attention models to a severe empirical testing [@mayo1991].

[^2]: **Look for more broad use of the theories. It is surely there,
    they are popular.**

Evidence for attentional mechanisms in blocking comes from several lines
of research, including experimental manipulations of cue competition
[@lepelley2007; @beesley2011], eye-tracking studies of overt attention
[@kruschke2005; @wills2007; @lepelley2007], behavioural measures of
attentional bias [@liu2013; @luque2018], and computational simulations
of attentional learning models [@kruschke2005; @paskewitz2020;
@paskewitz2023; see also @sewell2012]. Building on recent simulation
work [@paskewitz2020], the present study designs an experimental
procedure aimed at testing key predictions of learned-attention theories
about blocking and its relation to attention.

In the animal learning literature, blocking is widely regarded as a
cornerstone phenomenon, prompting strong claims such as that *"\[n\]o
empirical finding in the study of animal learning has been of greater
theoretical importance than the phenomenon of blocking."*
[@williams1999] However, despite its apparent robustness and the large
body of supporting evidence, @maes2016 were unable to detect the effect
across fifteen replications of previously published rodent paradigms
(see @soto2018 and @maes2018 for discussion of the implications of these
findings). Given this elusive nature of the blocking phenomenon even in
tightly controlled animal studies, it follows that any attempt to extend
blocking paradigms in human contingency learning should be preceded by a
rigorous replication of the original effect.

## Study designs {#sec-designs}

Although blocking is often treated as a single phenomenon, it can be
elicited using several related but methodologically distinct
experimental designs. These designs differ in how they set up cue
competition, control for confounds and what inferences they permit about
underlying mechanisms. @tbl-design-canonical summarises two
representative designs used in prior research [@kruschke2005;
@lepelley2007; @beesley2011; @sewell2012; @luque2018; see also
@paskewitz2020; @paskewitz2023].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-design-canonical
#| tbl-cap: Representative blocking experimental designs used by prior research.

blocking0$designs |>
  mutate(
    design = factor(
      case_when(
        design == "kruschke2005" ~ 1,
        design == "luque2018" ~ 2,
        .default = NA
      ),
      levels = 1:2,
      labels = c(
        "Canonical",
        "Novelty-controlled"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    across(ends_with("cue"), toupper)
  ) |>
  drop_na(design) |>
  arrange(design) |>
  select(!starts_with("stage3")) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "design") |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "---") |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 1", columns = starts_with("stage1")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 2", columns = starts_with("stage2")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Test", columns = starts_with("test")) |>
  cols_label(
    ends_with("cue") ~ "Cues",
    ends_with("outcome") ~ "Outcome",
    ends_with("preference") ~ "Preferred"
  ) |>
  catlasr::apa_style()
```

The **canonical blocking design** [e.g., @kruschke2005; @sewell2012]
captures the core logic of the phenomenon. In Stage 1, a (blocking) cue
A is established as a reliable predictor of an outcome (o1). In Stage 2,
A is presented in compound with a novel (blocked) cue B, paired with the
same outcome. Although B is a valid predictor of o1, it is redundant
because A already fully predicts the outcome. In a subsequent Test
stage, participants are asked to choose between the outcome (o1)
associated with the blocked cue B and an alternative outcome (o2)
associated with a control cue D, which was not paired with a pretrained
predictor. Participants typically prefer the outcome associated with the
control cue. This difference constitutes the canonical blocking effect.

Despite its conceptual simplicity, this design is partially confounded
by **cue novelty**. Specifically, the blocked cue B is introduced
alongside a well-established predictor (A), whereas the control cue D is
paired with another novel cue (C). This asymmetry makes it difficult to
determine whether reduced learning about B reflects blocking per se or
differences in how novel cues are processed within a compound.

One approach to addressing this limitation is to introduce the
competitor of the control cue during Stage 1 as a non-predictive
pretrained stimulus [e.g., @luque2018]. This manipulation equates
novelty across conditions, as both blocked and control cues are paired
with pretrained stimuli. However, this solution introduces a different
potential confound, as the control cue may appear more predictive by
virtue of being compared with a known non-predictive cue, thereby
inflating the apparent blocking effect (B-minus-D) without necessarily
engaging the same underlying mechanisms.

A further limitation shared by both designs is that blocked and control
cues are consistently paired with the same outcomes. While this allows
for strong conclusions about specific cue–outcome associations, it
provides limited insight into **cue-specific processing**. In
particular, blocking effects observed in these paradigms may arise from
interference of cue-outcome associations (e.g., A-o1 interfering with
B-o1 learning or memory) without requiring any change in the processing
of the blocked cue itself.

To address these issues, @lepelley2007 introduced a **three-stage**
design in which both blocked and control cues are subsequently paired
with novel outcomes in Stage 3, in the absence of previously trained
competitors (see @tbl-design-three-stage). This modification has two
important consequences.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-design-three-stage
#| tbl-cap: The three-stage experimental design for studying blocking.

blocking0$designs |>
  mutate(across(ends_with("cue"), toupper)) |>
  filter(design == "lepelley2007") |>
  select(-design) |>
  gt() |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "---") |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 1", columns = starts_with("stage1")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 2", columns = starts_with("stage2")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 3", columns = starts_with("stage3")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Test", columns = starts_with("test")) |>
  cols_label(
    ends_with("cue") ~ "Cues",
    ends_with("outcome") ~ "Outcome",
    ends_with("preference") ~ "Preferred"
  ) |>
  catlasr::apa_style()
```

First, it attenuates the novelty confound. Because all critical cues are
paired with new outcomes in Stage 3, and have comparable prior exposure,
differences in learning are less readily attributable to novelty.
Second, and more importantly, the design provides a more severe test of
attentional accounts. By requiring previously blocked and control cues
to support new learning, the design creates conditions under which any
deficit in processing of blocked cues must generalise beyond the
original contingency.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the three-stage design
places stronger constraints on theoretical accounts of blocking than
canonical paradigms. In particular, it creates conditions under which
attentional mechanisms are not merely sufficient but necessary to
explain the data within a well-specified computational framework.
Building on this logic, the present study adopts and extends this design
to directly contrast predictions derived from competing attentional
mechanisms. In particular, this increased severity becomes evident when
evaluating formal models of learning, as discussed in the following
section.

## Computational modelling {#sec-compmods}

Blocking elicited by the canonical design can be explained by *standard*
associative learning models without attentional components. For
instance, @sewell2012 showed that when fitting the EXIT model
[@kruschke2001] to data from the canonical blocking paradigm, the
best-fitting attention parameters shrank toward zero, effectively
reducing EXIT to the Rescorla–Wagner model [@rescorla1972]. In other
words, the canonical design can be accommodated without invoking
attentional mechanisms, even when such mechanisms are formally available
within the model [however, cf. @liu2013].

By contrast, *attention* is a necessary mechanism for associative models
to account for blocking elicited by the three-stage paradigm.
@paskewitz2020 showed that within this paradigm, the EXIT model fails to
reproduce blocking unless it includes at least one attentional mechanism
(either rapid attentional shifts or attentional competition).
Critically, when these mechanisms are combined, the model becomes overly
flexible. Unlike its single-mechanism submodels, the full model can
generate both the empirically observed pattern as well as its reversal.

Rapid attentional shifting and attentional competition are thus best
viewed as competing explanations of blocking, rather than complementary
components of a single process. @paskewitz2020 propose a modification of
the three-stage blocking paradigm designed to differentiate between
these two accounts. However, empirical tests capable of doing so are
still lacking.

## Experiment 1 (replication) {#sec-online-replication}

The three-stage procedure used to evaluate mechanisms of blocking by
@paskewitz2020 was originally introduced by @lepelley2007. Later,
@beesley2011 combined this design with eye-tracking to provide more
direct evidence of reduced overt attention to blocked stimuli during
both compound learning (Stage 2) and subsequent novel learning (Stage
3).

Accordingly, we first aim to replicate the findings of @beesley2011 and
then extend their experimental design following modifications proposed
by @paskewitz2020. Because these modifications concern behavioural
predictions and do not directly involve eye-tracking, we focus initially
on replicating and extending behavioural patterns of the three-stage
blocking paradigm. This approach allows us to leverage online sampling
to substantially increase statistical efficiency before moving to more
controlled laboratory studies.

### Procedure {#sec-online-replication-procedure}

In this study, we closely follow the procedure used by @beesley2011,
which was a variant of the allergy prediction task [@dickinson1996; 
@lochmann2003]. Each trial consisted of presenting a case of a
fictitious patient taking a vitamin pill containing certain chemicals
(*cues*), and asking the participant which of two possible side effects
(*outcomes*) the patient would suffer.

The overall study design followed the three-stage paradigm shown in
@tbl-design-three-stage, with chemicals randomly assigned to cues
$A-\beta$, and side effects randomly assigned to outcomes $o1-o4$,
independently for each participant. Critically, not only did the
outcomes change between Stages 2 (compound learning) and 3 (novel
learning), but Stage 3 also introduced a new patient, Mr. Y, replacing
the previous patient, Mr. X.

Stages 1–3 consisted of 10, 8, and 6 blocks, respectively, with each
block containing one instance of each of the eight stage-specific trial
types. Trial types were randomised independently for each participant
within each block, with the constraint that no trial type could be
repeated consecutively across block boundaries.

During the training stages (Stages 1–3; pre-training, compound learning,
and novel learning, respectively), participants received immediate
feedback about the correctness of their responses to facilitate
learning. In the test phase, participants were presented with two
chemicals and first selected the side effect they believed the patient
would suffer, followed by a confidence rating for that judgement. No
feedback was provided during the test phase.

### Stimuli {#sec-online-replication-stimuli}

Cues ($A-\beta$) were randomly assigned names of 28 fictitious
chemicals, separately for each participant. Because @beesley2011 do not
provide a full list of chemicals used in their experiment, we used the
available list from @lepelley2007, which employed a similar three-stage
paradigm. As in @beesley2011, the following four side effects were
randomly assigned to outcomes, separately for each participant:
dizziness, itchiness, headache, and nausea. Outcomes $o1$ and $o2$ were
always paired with Mr. X, whereas outcomes $o3$ and $o4$ were paired
with Mr. Y.

Cue stimuli consisted of words accompanied by a flask icon presented at
the top of the screen ***(NOTE: give later more precise specification,
either here or in appendix)***. Each training trial displayed either a
single, horizontally centred chemical name (Stage 1) or two chemical
names presented side-by-side (Stages 2–3), separated by ***some number
of pixels*** and joined by a horizontally centred "&" symbol indicating
a compound cue. The left–right order of cues in Stages 2–3 ***(NOTE: the
test phase ... TBA)*** was counterbalanced within participants across
blocks.

At the vertical midline, a prompt reading *"Which of the following
reactions did the patient have?"* was displayed, followed by the
instruction *"Click the picture of the reaction that you think, then
click the OK button"* on the next line.

At the bottom of the screen, two images of the same patient (Mr. X in
Stages 1–2; Mr. Y in Stage 3 and the test phase) were presented, each
depicting one of the two possible side effects corresponding to the
outcomes. The left–right mapping of outcomes was fixed, with outcomes
$o1$ and $o3$ always presented on the left, and outcomes $o2$ and $o4$
on the right. An OK button was displayed between the two images, centred
horizontally. ***NOTE: Both images were generated by ... TBA.***

Participants selected their response by clicking on the image
corresponding to the side effect they believed the patient would suffer.
Upon selection, the chosen image was highlighted with a thin black
frame. After confirming their choice by clicking the OK button, the
response was recorded.

During training stages, feedback was provided immediately after each
response. The word "Correct" (in green) was displayed following correct
responses, and "Wrong" (in red) following incorrect responses, replacing
the OK button. The correct response was additionally highlighted with a
thick blue frame.

In the test phase, responses were collected in the same manner, but no
feedback was provided. Instead, after each response, participants were
asked to rate their confidence on a scale from 1 ("Not confident at
all") to 10 ("Very confident"). Each of the eight test trial types was
presented twice in random order, with left–right configuration of cues
counterbalanced independently for each participant. ***(NOTE:
@beesley2011 presented each trial only once—reconsider whether the
second presentation is justified; although it occurs after training, it
may still introduce dependencies)***

## Eperiment 2 (extension) {#sec-online-extension}

@tbl-blocking-extension shows the experimental design of @beesley2011
after changes .

```{r}
#| label: tbl-blocking-extension
#| tbl-cap: Associational blocking experimental designs proposed by @paskewitz2020.

tibble(
  stage_1_cue = c("A", "C", "E", "G", "I", "L", "O", "R"),
  stage_1_out = paste0("o", rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2)),
  stage_2_cue = c("AB", "CD", "EF", "GH", "JK", "MN", "PQ", "ST"),
  stage_2_out = paste0("o", rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2)),
  stage_3_cue = c("BU", "DV", "FW", "HX", rep(NA, 4)),
  stage_3_out = paste0("o", c(rep(3:4, 2), rep(NA, 4))),
  test_cue = c("BX", "DW", "FV", "HU", "BV", "DU", "FX", "HW"),
  test_out = "?",
  test_pred_shift = paste0("o", rep(3:4, 4)),
  test_pred_comp = paste0("o", rep(4:3, 4))
) |>
  gt() |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 1", columns = starts_with("stage_1")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 2", columns = starts_with("stage_2")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 3", columns = starts_with("stage_3")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Model Predictions", columns = contains("pred")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Test", columns = starts_with("test")) |>
  cols_label(
    ends_with("cue") ~ "Cues",
    ends_with("out") ~ "Outcome",
    ends_with("shift") ~ "Shifting (RSWAC)",
    ends_with("comp") ~ "Competition\n(CompAct)"
  ) |>
  catlasr::apa_style()
```
